data.name: Sigil
data.description: Local-first C++20 signal daemon with a lock-free signal bus and rule engine connecting sensor/event sources to actions entirely on-device, no cloud round-trip.
data.tagline: A local-first signal daemon that connects real-world events to real-world actions, entirely on-device.
data.importance: Sigil is a systems-programming project, not a scripted demo: it's built around a lock-free concurrent ring buffer, a plugin architecture, and a real-time rule engine, all running with zero cloud dependency. That combination of concurrency correctness and hardware-adjacent design is the kind of work that separates application code from infrastructure code.
highlights: Designed a bounded, lock-free multi-producer/single-consumer ring buffer (the SignalBus) so concurrent source threads never block the rule engine, or each other
Built a plugin architecture (SourceBase / ActionBase) so a new sensor or a new effect can be added without touching the core engine at all
Implemented a rule engine with per-rule cooldowns, preventing a single noisy source from flooding the system with repeat alerts
Wrote a full GoogleTest suite covering every module, including a multi-threaded mock source that exercises the bus's concurrent-producer path outside of a single-threaded test
Scoped and documented a computer-vision extension (a camera source running on-device anomaly detection, trained on synthetically composited defect images) as the pipeline's next stress test

images.caption: The four layers: sources publish SignalEvents onto a lock-free bus, the rule engine drains it, and matching rules fire actions.
A real run of the daemon with the mock sources, followed by the GoogleTest suite: 42 of 42 tests passing.

howItWorks.title: One event shape for every input
howItWorks.body: A polled humidity sensor and a motion detector running on its own thread both produce the same SignalEvent: a source name, a field, a value (float, string or bool), a timestamp and a metadata map. Nothing downstream needs to know which device produced it.

howItWorks.title: A bus no thread has to wait on
howItWorks.body: Events go onto the SignalBus, a bounded ring buffer that many producer threads write to while a single consumer reads. Slots are claimed with atomic operations instead of a mutex, so a slow source never stalls the rule engine. When the ring is full, publish() returns false instead of overwriting older events.

howItWorks.title: Rules decide what matters
howItWorks.body: The rule engine drains the bus and checks each event against registered rules, for example humidity > 70 with a 30-second cooldown, so one noisy sensor can't fire the same alert on every reading.

howItWorks.title: Actions are plugins
howItWorks.body: A match becomes an ActionRequest sent to an ActionBase plugin, which fills placeholders such as {value} from the triggering event and runs. Today that prints to the console; GPIO pins and notifications are the next plugins. New sources and actions are added without touching the core.

data.name: HotelOps
data.description: Digital operations platform for a hotel chain: real-time room status board, GPS-verified staff clock-in, linen tracking, and cross-device sync across manager and housekeeping apps, replacing Excel sheets and a magnetic scheduling board.
data.tagline: A digital operations platform replacing a hotel chain's Excel sheets, magnetic scheduling board, and paper linen logs with one connected system.
data.importance: This is real production software for a real hotel chain (Fullon Hotels and Resorts), built to model operational constraints that don't show up in a typical CRUD tutorial: crew-based room assignment instead of one-person-per-room, role-based data visibility enforced at the database layer, and attendance that can't be spoofed from a phone.
highlights: Architected the database schema and row-level security policy layer so managers, housekeepers, and laundry staff each see exactly the data their role should, enforced by Postgres itself rather than hidden in the UI

Built a real-time room status board (Supabase Realtime) with per-team progress tracking and an availability-aware scheduling flow that a database trigger enforces server-side, not just client-side validation
Designed a priority-scoring engine that ranks dirty and in-progress rooms by proximity to check-in time, automatically driving the housekeeping task queue
Implemented GPS-verified clock-in through a server-side Postgres RPC function, so attendance can't be faked from the device

Shipped one shared codebase across a manager app (Vite + React, wrapped natively via Tauri) and a housekeeping app (Expo / React Native), both consuming the same Supabase client and TypeScript types so the two can't silently drift out of sync

images.caption: Architecture: a manager desktop app and a housekeeping mobile app share TypeScript types and one Supabase client, and Postgres enforces what each role can access.
A housekeeping day, from marking availability to a clean room, plus how room priority and role visibility are decided.

howItWorks.title: Replacing paper with one data model
howItWorks.body: The hotel ran on an Excel room grid, a magnetic scheduling board and paper linen sheets. HotelOps models all of it as Postgres tables (rooms, staff, teams, shifts, linen, room materials, incidents and messages), built up through 28 versioned migrations.

howItWorks.title: Teams form day by day
howItWorks.body: Housekeeping works as crews covering floors, not one person per room. Who is on a team is decided by that day's shifts, and a manager can only schedule someone on a day they marked available. A database trigger rejects anything else.

howItWorks.title: The rules live in the database
howItWorks.body: Row-level security decides what each role can read and write: managers see everything, housekeepers only the rooms on the floors their team covers today, and laundry only linen. Because Postgres enforces it, a modified app still can't see more.

howItWorks.title: Server-side checks where a phone can't be trusted
howItWorks.body: Clock-in sends the phone's GPS position to a Postgres function that verifies it, so attendance can't be faked. A trigger gives each room that still needs cleaning a priority score from 0 to 100 based on how close its next check-in is, which orders the housekeepers' queue.

howItWorks.title: Live on every screen
howItWorks.body: Status changes stream through Supabase Realtime, so the manager's floor board updates as rooms move from Dirty to In progress to Clean. Both apps import the same shared types, and the desktop app also ships as a native macOS app through Tauri.

data.name: NDHU Task Management
data.description: Full-stack mobile task management app with a local-first Expo/React Native client with offline SQLite sync, and a C++ (Drogon) REST API backend with JWT auth and automatic Moodle LMS assignment import.
data.tagline: A local-first mobile task manager that syncs cleanly across devices and pulls assignments straight from Moodle automatically.
data.importance: Cross-device sync is a genuinely hard distributed-systems problem, and this project solves it correctly rather than papering over it: a custom conflict-resolution protocol distinguishes fields a user owns from fields only Moodle should own, so a stale device can never silently overwrite a teammate's fresher data.
highlights: Designed and implemented a two-way sync protocol between an offline-first SQLite client and a C++/Drogon backend, using per-row dirty flags and server timestamps to reconcile edits from multiple devices

Solved a subtle identity problem unique to Moodle-imported tasks (every device independently discovers the same assignment and mints its own local ID for it) by introducing a stable moodle_event_id as the real cross-device key, with field-level write protection so a stale device can't clobber a fresher one
Built a rich-text note editor as a WebView/contenteditable hybrid to support inline images, audio attachments, and links, capabilities a plain React Native text input can't offer
Hardened the system with RS256 JWT auth and revocation, AES-256-GCM at-rest encryption for stored Moodle session tokens, and hybrid RSA-OAEP for password transport

Added a CI pipeline (typecheck, lint, and tests gating every deploy) and a real test suite to a codebase that had neither, and deleted roughly 1,900 lines of dead code found during a structural review pass

images.caption: Sign-in with Moodle credentials, the task list with Moodle assignments imported automatically, the calendar, and a task's detail sheet.
A day's agenda, the create menu, the new-task sheet, and a task with file and photo attachments.
How two phones on the same account stay in sync without overwriting each other's changes.

howItWorks.title: Offline first
howItWorks.body: Every screen reads from and writes to a SQLite database on the phone, so the app works with no network at all. The server is only needed to fetch Moodle assignments and to let a user's devices reconcile.

howItWorks.title: Moodle comes to you
howItWorks.body: The C++ server signs in to Moodle on the user's behalf, with the session stored encrypted (AES-256-GCM), and scrapes assignments. A background worker re-polls on an interval and sends push notifications for new or changed ones.

howItWorks.title: Sync in one round trip
howItWorks.body: Every local edit marks its row dirty. On sync, the phone pushes its dirty rows; the server keeps an incoming row only if it is newer than the stored one, then returns everything other devices changed since this phone last synced, stamped with the server's own clock.

howItWorks.title: Two kinds of task, two sets of rules
howItWorks.body: A task the user typed has one ID created by one device, so every field syncs. A Moodle assignment is discovered separately by each device, so it is matched by Moodle's own event ID instead, and only user-owned fields (done, pinned, notes) can be pushed. A stale phone can never overwrite a fresher title or due date.

howItWorks.title: Rich notes
howItWorks.body: Notes are edited in a WebView running a custom contenteditable editor, which is what allows inline images, audio recordings, links and formatting that a native text field can't provide.

data.name: Maestro
data.description: Two-stream BiLSTM real-time hand-gesture recognition system for hands-free presentation control, with a MediaPipe Hands feature pipeline, PySide6 control UI, and cross-platform packaged app. Winner of the NDHU Undergraduate Project Excellent Award, 2026.
data.tagline: A production-grade, real-time hand-gesture recognition system that turns a webcam into a hands-free presentation remote.
data.importance: Winner of NDHU's Undergraduate Project Excellent Award, 2026. Runs real-time inference on ordinary consumer laptops with no GPU, packaged as a genuine cross-platform desktop app rather than a notebook demo, which is precisely the gap between a machine learning experiment and a machine learning product.
highlights: Built a two-stream LSTM classifier recognizing a 10-class gesture vocabulary (a hybrid of the Jester and IPN datasets) from MediaPipe Hands landmarks, running in real time on CPU alone

Designed the full inference pipeline end to end: camera capture, hand selection, feature engineering, a sliding-window buffer, prediction stabilization, and command dispatch straight to OS-level keyboard and pointer events

Built a non-blocking PySide6 control UI, with inference running in a background QThread and state updates throttled to roughly 10Hz over Qt signals, so the interface never stutters the model or vice versa
Packaged and distributed standalone installers for macOS and Windows with the trained model bundled directly into the app, no Python runtime or internet connection required to run it

images.caption: The inference pipeline, and the 10-class gesture vocabulary with the command each gesture triggers.
The PySide6 control app during a session: live mode, detected gesture, confidence, FPS and latency, with the event log below.
Settings for the camera, window length and step, validity ratio and command cooldown, all editable from the app.
Normalized confusion matrix on the hybrid test set: every gesture class at 0.94 or higher.
Per-clip inference latency against RGB video models on the IPN Hand benchmark: the landmark-based model is the fastest at 3.1 ms.

howItWorks.title: From pixels to landmarks
howItWorks.body: Each webcam frame goes through MediaPipe Hands, which returns 21 keypoints per hand. Working on keypoints instead of raw video is what keeps the model small enough for a laptop CPU.

howItWorks.title: Motion, not a single pose
howItWorks.body: The system picks the active hand, normalizes its landmarks into features and keeps a sliding window of recent frames (24 frames, advancing 3 at a time), so the model sees how the hand moves.

howItWorks.title: Two-stream LSTM
howItWorks.body: A two-stream LSTM classifies each window into one of 10 classes: nine gestures plus an 'unknown' class that absorbs ordinary hand movement so it doesn't trigger anything.

howItWorks.title: Act only when sure
howItWorks.body: Predictions are stabilized over time and pass through an activation controller with confidence thresholds and a cooldown before they become real keyboard and pointer events: swipes change slides, pointing drives a laser pointer or a pen.

howItWorks.title: A real desktop app
howItWorks.body: The PySide6 interface runs inference in a background thread and receives updates about 10 times a second, so neither blocks the other. Installers for macOS and Windows bundle the trained model, with no Python or internet connection needed.

data.name: NDHU Second-Hand Book Store
data.description: Campus marketplace for NDHU students to buy and sell used textbooks. Led the Go/Fiber backend architecture and REST API design end to end, and integrated an AI-based book condition classification model into the pipeline.
data.tagline: A campus marketplace where NDHU students buy and sell used textbooks, with AI-assisted condition grading.
data.importance: A full team software-engineering project, built from a blank repository to a working three-service system across a semester. Owning the backend architecture on a team project means design decisions have to be explained and defended to teammates, not just made in isolation, a different and harder skill than solo development.
highlights: Owned the Go/Fiber backend architecture end to end: REST API design, service logic, and database schema, integrated with a TypeScript/Next.js frontend and a separate Python AI microservice
Built the AI-based book condition classification model that plugs into the listing pipeline, automating a step sellers would otherwise have to do by hand
Set up the full local and staging Docker Compose stack behind Traefik, plus CI that lints, tests, and builds every pull request and an automated staging deploy on merge to main

images.caption: Architecture: a Next.js client, a Go/Fiber API and a Python AI service, routed through Traefik and run together with Docker Compose.
How a listing's photos become a condition label: detected defects are weighted by severity, and the worst photo decides.

howItWorks.title: Sign in as a student
howItWorks.body: Students sign in through NDHU's own CAS single sign-on. The API validates the CAS ticket server to server, creates the account on first login and issues a JWT that middleware checks on every protected route.

howItWorks.title: List a book
howItWorks.body: Photos are uploaded first and registered in an images table, and the listing then references them. Listings come back with all their image URLs aggregated in a single SQL query instead of one extra query per image.

howItWorks.title: Grade its condition
howItWorks.body: The API forwards the photos to the internal AI service. An object-detection model finds defects such as tears, stains and creases, each weighted by severity and confidence. The worst photo sets the score, and the book is labeled good, moderate or poor.

howItWorks.title: Buy it safely
howItWorks.body: Adding to the cart is idempotent. Checkout locks the selected listings with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE so two buyers can't purchase the same copy, and stores the price paid on each order line so receipts stay correct if a seller later edits the listing.

data.name: JsonFS
data.description: C++ FUSE virtual filesystem that mounts JSON files and live REST APIs as a navigable POSIX directory tree, with schema-enforced writes rejected at the syscall layer, atomic write-back, and live URL mounting with TTL refresh.
data.tagline: A FUSE filesystem that turns any JSON file or live REST API into a navigable, writable POSIX directory tree.
data.importance: Unix's "everything is a file" philosophy was never extended to structured data, so JsonFS extends it: grep, diff, watch, and every other Unix tool start working on live JSON with zero glue code. It's novel in three specific ways beyond prior JSON-FUSE projects: live URL mounting with TTL refresh, structural diffing on every refresh, and schema enforcement at the syscall layer rather than in application code.
highlights: Implemented schema-enforced writes inside the FUSE write() callback itself, so an invalid value is rejected with a syscall-level EINVAL before any application code ever sees it, and deleting a required field is blocked at unlink()

Built live HTTP/HTTPS mounting with configurable TTL refresh, giving a REST endpoint a stable, composable mountpoint that grep, watch, and shell pipelines can use directly, something a one-shot `watch curl | jq` can't do
Designed atomic write-back (write-to-temp, then rename) so a crash mid-write can never corrupt the source file
Wrote 55 unit tests across 6 GoogleTest suites and full Doxygen documentation of the architecture and concurrency design

images.caption: Each JSON object becomes a directory and each value a file. Reads go through a TTL cache; writes are validated against the schema, then saved atomically.
A real session on Linux: Unix tools read the data, a valid write lands in config.json, and invalid writes are refused with EINVAL.

howItWorks.title: JSON as a tree of files
howItWorks.body: JsonFS parses the source into an in-memory tree. Objects and arrays become directories (array items are named 0, 1, 2, and so on) and every leaf value becomes a small file whose content is that value as text.

howItWorks.title: The kernel asks, JsonFS answers
howItWorks.body: It is a FUSE filesystem: when any program opens, reads or writes a path under the mountpoint, the kernel forwards the call to JsonFS. Thin C callbacks hand each call to one C++ class, which looks the path up in the tree.

howItWorks.title: Live sources with a TTL
howItWorks.body: The source can be a local file or an HTTP(S) URL. A thread-safe TTL cache decides when the data is stale, and the next read after that refetches the source and rebuilds the tree, so watch cat on a mounted API always shows a recent value.

howItWorks.title: Validated, crash-safe writes
howItWorks.body: With --schema, every write is checked against the JSON Schema inside the write() callback (type, range, enum, pattern, required). A bad value returns EINVAL to the shell before anything changes. A good value is written to a temporary file that is then renamed over the original, so a crash can never leave half-written JSON.

data.name: Robot Arm Load Analyzer
data.description: Real-time humanoid robot simulator that answers whether a pose and payload overload any joint: a from-scratch C++ physics engine (DH kinematics, Jacobian statics, Recursive Newton-Euler dynamics), a PyTorch neural surrogate benchmarked against it, and a grasp planner that picks objects up, all in a Qt Quick 3D interface driven with the mouse.
data.tagline: Can this robot hold that weight, in that pose, without overloading a joint, and can it go and pick the object up? Ask it live, in 3D.
data.importance: Every real robot has to answer this question at design time, and the answer is usually a number printed once on a spec sheet. Here it is live: drag the robot, change a mass, and every joint's load updates. The physics underneath is derived by hand and cross-checked, not borrowed from a robotics library, and the neural network's speed-up is measured by the app itself, not claimed. Kinematics, learning, search and planning all meet in one working system instead of separate exercises.
highlights: Derived and implemented forward and inverse kinematics, Jacobian statics and full Recursive Newton-Euler dynamics from first principles in C++17 and Eigen, cross-checked against an independent virtual-work derivation

Trained a PyTorch MLP surrogate on 30,000 poses labeled by the exact engine and ran it through a hand-written C++ forward pass with no ML runtime, measuring about a 9x speed-up in the app's own payload-capacity scan

Built a grasp planner that searches whole-body poses (waist, lift, hip lean, arm), rejects any that break joint or torque limits, and executes approach, grasp, lift and carry with smooth, speed-limited motion
Built the Qt Quick 3D interface from procedural meshes placed by forward kinematics, with click-and-drag control of the hand, every joint, the torso and the lift

Backed it with 256 GoogleTest cases in 20 suites, including whole pick-and-place sequences for every object type; one deliberately orthogonal test caught a silent sign bug in the hand-derived dynamics that two other tests missed

images.caption: The robot among furniture and objects. Each joint's gauge shows its live load against its torque limit.
A planned pick-and-place: reach the bottle, grasp and lift it, lean over the table, set it down upright and return home.
Arm straight out holding 14 kg: every joint is past its limit and turns red.
Payload capacity scan from stretched out to folded: exact physics and the neural network on the same chart, with measured run times.
The 17-joint hand closing around a bottle.
Switched to a five-joint warehouse arm with a two-finger gripper, holding a can it picked from above.
Dragging the hand: the waist turns, the lift lowers and the torso leans so the hand can reach the point.

howItWorks.title: Exact physics from first principles
howItWorks.body: Each arm joint is described with Denavit-Hartenberg parameters. Forward kinematics chains the transforms, the Jacobian turns link weights and the payload into the torque every joint must hold, and a full Recursive Newton-Euler pass adds inertia and Coriolis terms when the arm moves. All of it is hand-written C++ with Eigen.

howItWorks.title: A neural network that imitates it
howItWorks.body: A C++ generator samples 30,000 random poses and payloads and labels them with the exact engine. A small PyTorch MLP learns pose + payload to torques; its weights are exported to JSON and run by a hand-written C++ forward pass, about 9x faster in the app's own scan (0.57 ms vs 5.19 ms for 40 poses). Change the arm's geometry and AI mode switches itself off, because the network was trained for a different arm.

howItWorks.title: Planning a pick-up
howItWorks.body: Click an object and the planner searches a grid of lift heights and hip leans, solves the arm's joint angles for each (closed-form for the humanoid arm, damped least squares otherwise), rejects poses that break joint or torque limits, and keeps the one that loads the joints least. If none works, it says which joint would be overloaded.

howItWorks.title: Acting it out
howItWorks.body: The pick-up runs as sub-goals (approach, grasp, lift, carry) with smooth, speed-limited motion. While the robot holds an object, that object's mass is the payload, so every gauge shows what it is really carrying.

howItWorks.title: Built in Qt Quick 3D
howItWorks.body: The robot, furniture and objects are procedural meshes positioned by forward kinematics, and the C++ controllers are exposed to QML as a module. 256 GoogleTest cases in 20 suites cover the physics and whole pick-and-place sequences.
